name: HPV Vaccination Coverage and Policy Implementation
anchorClaim: HPV vaccination coverage among university-age and catch-up-eligible populations remains below public-health targets and varies by at least [X] percentage points between the highest and lowest coverage regions, as documented in epidemiological surveillance and policy-implementation studies.
plainQuestion: HPV vaccination coverage among university-age and catch-up-eligible populations falls short of public-health targets, and varies widely from one region to another.
confidenceSummary: The Grade F is a caution about quality: the studies support the general picture that coverage falls short of target rather than the specific size of the gap, and most rest on brief summaries rather than full papers.

guide.whatScienceSays: DATOM looked at 45 studies that directly tested this claim. All 45 support the idea that HPV vaccination coverage among university-age and catch-up-eligible groups falls short of public-health targets and varies widely from region to region; none pointed the other way. So the clear findings back the claim, which is what the "Supported" verdict below means. But the Grade F beside it matters just as much: the evidence is weak in quality even though it points one way, so treat this as the current direction, not a settled, high-certainty result. Many more studies touched on the topic without testing this exact claim; they appear further down, tagged by what they looked at.
guide.howConfident:
DATOM gives this claim a confidence score of 20 out of 100, which we call Speculative. That's true even though 74% of the 196 sources point the same direction and none disagree with it. That's a big gap between how much the sources agree and how confident the score is.

Here's why: the confidence score isn't about whether studies agree on the general idea. It's about whether the evidence can back up one specific, citable number. This claim has a blank spot built into it: it talks about an "[X] percentage point" gap in coverage, but no study here, and no combination of them, has produced one agreed number to fill that blank.

The way the studies were done makes this worse. Across only 196 sources, there are 123 different ways the methods were described, and 79 of those descriptions are each used only once. That means a Belgian disease-spread model, a US insurance-claims study, and a Rhode Island survey are all being counted as evidence for the same claim. But they were built in completely different ways, and several of them didn't report how many people or samples they studied.

On top of that, 133 of the 196 sources (68%) are based only on abstracts, the short summary of a study, rather than the full published paper. That limits how much of each study's actual method DATOM could check. And all 196 sources are still waiting for a human reviewer to check them; none has been verified yet.

Strong agreement on direction, combined with an unanswered core question and evidence that hasn't been checked yet, is exactly the pattern that produces a low confidence score even when the support percentage looks high.
decisionSupport: Don't quote one single national number for the coverage gap. The claim's own "[X] percentage point" blank was never filled in. And the two clearest regional findings in our sources don't even agree on scale: Belgium shows a 54 to 61 point gap (about 90% coverage in Flanders versus 29 to 36% in Wallonia-Brussels), while France's national full-course rate is flat at 18.6%, less than a third of its own 60% target.

If you're using this for outreach or policy, split people by whether they're in the "catch-up" age group, not just by age alone. A US study of 118 million people with commercial insurance found that uptake among the 22-and-older catch-up group had dropped to 1% or less by 2016. That's not a sign of a new access problem. It's because teens are now getting vaccinated earlier, so fewer people need catching up later.

Treat coverage numbers from different studies as pointing in the same general direction, but don't average them together as if they measured the same thing. The methods behind the 196 sources were described in 123 different ways, 79 of which show up only once. They include disease-spread models, insurance-claims analyses, and one-time surveys, none of which were designed to be combined.

Give more weight to findings backed by a full published study rather than just a summary. 133 of the 196 sources (68%) are based only on the abstract, the short summary at the top of a paper, not the full paper itself. That means a good chunk of the 74% support figure rests on summary-level claims rather than a fully checked method.

Before citing any specific percentage from this claim in something high-stakes, flag it for a human reviewer to double check first. All 196 sources are still waiting for that review. On top of that, 15 sources are missing a DOI (a permanent link or ID for the study) and 3 don't list any authors, so we haven't fully confirmed where all of this evidence came from yet.
guide.faultLines:
There are three real weak spots in this evidence.

The Gap Size Was Never Pinned Down: the claim asks for one specific percentage-point number to fill in its "[X]" blank. But the 196 sources only support the general idea, that coverage is below target and varies by region, not any single agreed number. So the 74% support figure is really answering an easier question than the one the claim is actually asking.

No Two Studies Used the Same Method: the methods behind the 196 sources are described in 123 different ways, 79 of which appear only once. Several of the most solid supporting studies, including the ones from Belgium, Switzerland, and Rhode Island, simply list sample size as "Not reported." That makes it impossible to know how much weight each study's result actually deserves.

We Haven't Checked Everything Yet: 68% of the sources (133 of 196) are based only on abstracts rather than the full published study. All 196 are still waiting on human review. 15 are missing a DOI (a permanent study identifier), and 3 don't list any authors. On top of that, the sources span publication years 2011 to 2026, but 30% of them (59 of 196) were published in just 2025 and 2026 alone. That means the newest surveillance data is counted much more heavily than the older studies it's being lumped in with.

datoms.claim: HPV vaccination coverage among university-age and catch-up-eligible populations in Japan remains below public-health targets, with the highest cumulative vaccination rate at 33.6% for first dose among the FY2006 birth cohort as of June 2023.
datoms.source: Mahiro Sazawa, Chieko Ishiguro, W. Mimura, M. Maeda, Fumiko Murata "Impact of the resumption of proactive recommendation of HPV vaccination on HPV vaccination rates in Japan: an interrupted time series analysis based on the VENUS study" (2025). doi:10.1136/bmjph-2024-000982

datoms.claim: HPV vaccination coverage among boys aged 13-17 varies by rural-urban residence, with boys from isolated small rural towns showing lower initiation (17.3%) and completion (5.31%) rates compared to urban boys (28.7% and 10.7% respectively), representing a 11.4 percentage point difference in initiation.
datoms.source: Allison L. Swiecki‐Sikora, Kevin Henry, Deanna Kepka "HPV Vaccination Coverage Among US Teens Across the Rural‐Urban Continuum" (2019). doi:10.1111/jrh.12353

datoms.claim: HPV vaccination coverage for full-dose completion among girls aged 9-14 years is 47.6% (95% CI: 39.7%-57.4%), substantially below the 90% public-health target.
datoms.source: Han Jingjing, Li Zhang, Yuqing Chen, Yuelun Zhang, Le Wang "Global HPV vaccination programs and coverage rates: a systematic review" (2025). doi:10.1016/j.eclinm.2025.103290

datoms.claim: HPV vaccination coverage varies by jurisdiction, with differences ranging up to 48.4 percentage points for up-to-date status across selected state and local areas.
datoms.source: Laurie D. Elam–Evans, David Yankey, James A. Singleton, Natalie Sterrett, Lauri E. Markowitz "National, Regional, State, and Selected Local Area Vaccination Coverage Among Adolescents Aged 13–17 Years — United States, 2019" (2020). doi:10.15585/mmwr.mm6933a1

datoms.claim: HPV vaccination coverage rate in France is 17.2% in girls aged 16 years, which is substantially lower than the 70% coverage rate observed in other Western European countries.
datoms.source: M. Uhart, Marjorie Adam, André Dahlab, Xavier Bresse "Loss of chance associated with sub-optimal HPV vaccination coverage rate in France" (2017). doi:10.1016/j.pvr.2017.02.004

scope: Teens and young adults, ages 9 to 26, in the US, Belgium, France, Switzerland, Australia, and across Europe more broadly.
metric: How many people got the HPV vaccine and finished the full series, measured in percent, and how much coverage differs from one region to another, measured in percentage points.
